title: Buildings the seller had bought shortly before
question: In which purchases does the full roll history put the prior sale within one, two or three years of the public purchase, and which buildings show no prior sale date at all?
finding: The prior sale date falls within one year of the public purchase in 2 cases, within two in 5 and within three in 8; 3 of those are finished buildings comparable like for like: 681-687 Ellis Street (295 days, +39%); 1000 Sutter Street (Hotel Granada) (477 days, +53%); 888 Post Street (727 days, +190%). 3 more fall between three and four years. 12 matched purchases show no earlier sale date on any roll from 2007 to 2025; for 3 of them the land value was nonetheless re-set in some year, which means a change of ownership or reassessment the roll does not date.
how: The same purchases as the screen above. The prior sale is the latest sale date on any roll from 2007 to 2025 that falls before the public purchase (the date the City’s Board file was introduced; for the two nonprofit purchases, the purchase date the roll records). Each row says what the earlier three-roll screen could and could not show. A sale date that is the City’s own earlier purchase of a neighbouring lot is not counted. Buildings with no sale date are listed here only when the land value was re-set within three roll years before the purchase.
limits: The roll records no price. The value that appears after a sale date is an indicator of the price, because California law re-sets assessed value to the price paid when a property changes hands; exemptions, a transfer of part of a property, transfers the law excludes from reassessment and new construction all break that link. The recorded deed and its transfer-tax declaration at the Assessor-Recorder would settle what was paid; neither is open data. A short holding period has honest causes: a developer who bought a site, built and sold; a seller who renovated or changed the use; an owner who bought at a low point. Where the City buys land under a subsidised development from the partnership it also lends to, a recent sale date is how the deal is built. The roll names no owners: that the seller to the City bought on the prior sale date is an inference. Sale dates are unevenly kept: 49% of all parcels had no sale date on the 2007 roll and 31% on the 2025 roll, and the number of parcels whose sale date falls in the roll’s own year drops from a middle of 4,610 to 8 on the 2017 roll and 303 on the 2021 roll, so counts of sales cannot be compared across years and an absent date is not an absent sale.
